stories.title: 2-year-old who went missing in desert found by volunteer
stories.summary: A 2-year-old wandered into the Arizona desert wearing only a diaper and spent seven hours alone in the cold. More than 100 searchers, drones, and helicopters couldn't find her — but volunteer Jay Stewart did, spotting her curled under a bush just after midnight. Her tiny body was too cold for heat sensors to detect, making his on-foot discovery a genuine miracle.
stories.extended_summary: Jay Stewart had been walking the desert for three hours when he heard a small voice answer his call. He shined his flashlight on a bush, and a 2-year-old girl popped up. Vella Campillo had been missing for seven hours, wearing only a diaper, after wandering from her yard near Eloy, Arizona, just before sunset. More than 100 people joined the search, along with drones and helicopters — but her small body produced too little heat for thermal cameras to catch. Stewart, who responded to the sheriff's plea for volunteers, found her about a mile and a half from home. 'I grabbed her and picked her up and she was clinging to me so tight,' he said, calling it a life-changing moment.

Find one, keep it, and maybe rediscover why you love the outdoors in winter.
stories.extended_summary: Three hundred and fifty wooden ornaments, each shaped like Oregon with a red VW bus and Mount Hood on it, are hidden along more than 25 hiking trails across the state starting Nov. 20. It's the ninth year of the Willamette Valley Visitors Association's ornament hunt — a clever trick to get people onto muddy, rainy trails in the darkest months. The event has expanded from a single national forest to trails in Estacada, Mt. Hood, and the Willamette, Siuslaw, and Umpqua forests. About 30 volunteers hide the ornaments, and some, like Astoria's Melinda Martin, have done it all nine years. The full trail list drops Nov. 20 — bring boots.

stories.extended_summary: Before launching the Pocahontas Reframed Film Festival, director Bradby Brown sat down with the chiefs of all 11 state-recognized tribes in Virginia to make sure they were on board. The festival takes its name from the most recognized Native American woman in the country, and its mission is to reframe the story most people learned from a Disney movie. Deputies, search and rescue, and more than 40 community volunteers searched into the night; the next day a Montana Air National Guard helicopter spotted her sitting upright and in good spirits. Her husband Mark's emotional thank-you — and the 200 neighbors who showed up — says it all.

On Veterans Day, a Montana Air National Guard helicopter found her — sitting upright, in good spirits — and hoisted her into a Black Hawk for the trip to the hospital. Her husband Mark called into a local radio show, his voice breaking: 'Support your local search and rescue guys, and I want to say thanks.' He estimated over 200 neighbors had walked the area looking for her, and some brought food for the volunteers.
